canberra.title: Unverified website incorrectly claims Canberra school student killed in stabbing
canberra.snippet: A website has incorrectly claimed an Erindale College student had died following a stabbing at the school earlier on Wednesday (5 August)...
canberra.content:
5 August 2026

Start the conversation

No violent incident required a police presence at Erindale College on 5 August. Photo: Facebook.

A website has incorrectly claimed an Erindale College student had died following a stabbing at the school earlier on Wednesday (5 August).

The post was shared on Canberra Facebook noticeboards, stating a police investigation was underway.

“A student has died following a stabbing at Erindale College in Canberra on Wednesday, prompting a major emergency response and a police investigation,” it falsely stated.

“Emergency services, including ACT Policing and paramedics, responded to the incident at the college on McBryde crescent [sic] in Wanniassa.

“Authorities established a large police presence around the school as officers secured the scene … students were placed into lockdown while emergency responders and investigators worked to determine exactly what occurred.

“The fatal stabbing has shocked the school community, with many awaiting further information as police continue their investigation.”

All of this was incorrect.

Region has confirmed there was a police presence at Erindale College on Wednesday (5 August) morning but not because of a stabbing.

It’s understood the body of a missing man was found in the vicinity of the school.

Parents and students were alerted by the school that police needed to be present in the area.

“When entering and exiting our school today, please avoid the courtyard area while ACT Policing attend to an incident (not related to our school),” it stated.

“Please be assured there is no risk to safety. Thank you for your understanding.”

An Education Directorate spokesperson said families would always be alerted by their schools when needed

“ACT public schools will communicate with families as required in regard to incidents impacting school operations,” they said.

The article making the false claims had no attributed author.

canberra.title: Revenue ACT facing multiple actions over homebuyer concession reassessments
canberra.snippet: The ACT Revenue Office is facing a clutch of appeals against its retrospective stamp duty assessments, with many involving separated coup...
canberra.content:
The ACT Revenue Office continues to take a hard line despite the adverse reports. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

The ACT Revenue Office is facing a clutch of appeals against its retrospective stamp duty assessments, with many involving separated couples angry at how their eligibility for the Home Buyers Concession Scheme has been denied.

One involves a family which extricated their mother from a harmful marriage and has had to cope with her failing mental health and even a suicide attempt, while negotiating a payout to her ex-husband, selling the home and seeing her into a new one.

The appeals to the ACT Civil and Administrative Tribunal continue to flow five months after a damning report from the ACT Auditor-General found that the ACT Revenue Office failed to explain its complex eligibility requirements, relied on self-assessment and then pursued debtors without regard to their circumstances or financial situation.

It was revealed last year that the Revenue Office was chasing thousands of people who had inadvertently filled out their applications for stamp duty concessions incorrectly or were now deemed ineligible, sometimes years later.

The report echoed a Legislative Assembly committee inquiry that found the application process was unclear and the ACT Revenue Office was aggressive and inconsiderate in applying penalties and recovering debts.

Some have also accused the Revenue Office of nitpicking and finding technicalities to frustrate the intent of the stamp duty exemption for separating couples forced to sell their shared property and purchase anew as singles.

If there are family law orders or a binding financial agreement that includes the transfer of a property and results in one person relinquishing their interest in real estate to their former spouse, the government may waive the stamp duty payable on that person’s future home purchase.

One ACAT applicant who bought a home in 2022 after separating says the Revenue Office is asserting that these orders don’t count unless they were issued prior to the sale of the property with your former partner.

Jane (not her real name) said that at her directions hearing, the ACT Government Solicitor said the Revenue Office had recently made at least 11 decisions on this basis and had so far received three applications to ACAT, all of which had started recently.

The matters involve thousands of dollars in duty, interest and penalty tax.

She said the government solicitor intimated at the directions hearing that all of those decisions had been made on a similar basis – the commissioner had taken the view that because the court orders weren’t issued before the property was sold, they didn’t have any effect.

The other position the Revenue Office was taking was that if you willingly sold your property and the court didn’t “drag you kicking and screaming to do it”, the exemption was not available.

“The argument that I make is that there’s nothing to suggest that there’s that kind of timing requirement,” she said.

“It’s also not really clear how they identify what’s a voluntary or an involuntary transfer of property.

“If you’re breaking up with someone and you have to sell your shared house, I don’t really know how they distinguish at what point it’s involuntary.”

A lawyer herself in this field, she said the Revenue Office was misinterpreting the government instrument.

Jake is taking on the Revenue Office on behalf of his mother who, like many, was hit with a $21,000 bill years after the 2022 property purchase.

The Revenue Office had seized on the wording of the Consent Orders, which had been drafted to prevent the husband taking the property by saying Jake’s mother “may elect” to sell the home rather than has to sell the home, to argue it was not a forced sale.

Jake said that his brother had also paid the husband $100,000, as required by the orders, by a certain date because their mother had no money. He was reimbursed for this bridging finance when the property was sold and another property was purchased for his mother.

But the Revenue Office decision stated that once the $100,000 payment was made, a condition in the orders requiring the property to be sold to achieve this was not triggered.

“As a result, the consent orders did not require the taxpayer to sell the property,” it said.

“While the taxpayer has considered it necessary to sell the Ngunnawal property in order to reimburse your brother and manage her financial circumstances, those considerations arise from the taxpayer’s personal financial position rather than from any requirement imposed by the consent orders themselves.”

Jake said she had to sell the house anyway and the Revenue Office should have taken a broader view and looked at the whole situation, especially in light of a parliamentary inquiry finding.

All during this traumatic process, his mother’s mental health was failing with a suicide attempt and admissions to hospital, but the Revenue Office only paid lip service to a request for relief on compassionate grounds.

Jake said it was clear that the eligibility criteria were difficult to understand.

“Of course she thought she was eligible,” he said.

“We all thought she was eligible. This is why so many people have come forward. This is why there was a parliamentary inquiry into it.”

Both Jane and Jake said the issue had become a matter of principle.

“I want a record of this process, and I want to do whatever I can to just hold them to account,” Jake said.

canberra.title: Uproar after NSW Government offers to buy out South Coast commercial abalone shareholders
canberra.snippet: The abalone industry and Aboriginal cultural fishers are furious about the NSW Government’s offer to buy back shares at $6355 per s...
canberra.content:
NSW Minister for Agriculture Tara Moriarty announced the offer this week. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The abalone industry and Aboriginal cultural fishers are furious about the NSW Government’s offer to buy back shares at $6355 per share from commercial abalone fishers to address declining abalone numbers.

The area from near Bundeena to Red Point, south of Eden, will be closed to commercial abalone fishing from 1 July 2027 for an unspecified time.

A delicacy in Asia and a traditional Aboriginal food, abalone are under pressure from overfishing, diminishing kelp forests and climate change.

On 4 August NSW Minister for Agriculture Tara Moriarty announced the government is offering a voluntary share surrender program.

It follows an earlier announcement that the total allowable catch for blacklip abalone in 2026-27 was 52 tonnes, down 40 per cent from 2025-26.

To help commercial abalone fishers “transition”, the government will provide up to $9000 for training assistance to fishing business owners who surrender all their abalone shares, and up to $1000 per eligible fishing business owner for financial guidance regardless of whether or not they surrender shares.

Ms Moriarty said on radio she expected a “significant amount of people” will take up the share surrender option. A few weeks earlier the abalone industry rejected the government’s offer to buy back shares at $4221. Shares traded at $10,492 in 2018.

In a statement on 5 August, the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD) said the initial share surrender price was based on valuation advice by BDO Corporate Finance Australia. After shareholder consultation, the higher valuation of $6355 was adopted, “using more conservative and risk-averse assumptions about future returns and fishery performance”.

Second-generation diver Ryan Morris dives for abalone and the longspined sea urchins that are destroying the coast’s kelp forests.

Mr Morris said what the government was doing to commercial abalone fishers was “bordering on criminal”.

He said Minister Moriarty was being “very coy” about what the government will do with the shares. “Those shares should be ripped up, never to be used again, but she doesn’t want to have that,” he said.

Furthermore, the compensation only covered abalone shareholders, not the processors or divers who would become obsolete due to reduced abalone volumes, nor other businesses reliant on the industry.

He said the NSW Fisheries Department seemed unable to prosecute Indigenous fishers who he claimed were harvesting abalone illegally, beyond their cultural fishing rights. “The illegal fishing is already happening in Disaster Bay and Green Cape outside the Native Title area,” he said.

Mr Morris said the share buyback offer “sets a really bad precedent for commercial fishing in this state”. He is also concerned about the implications for NSW’s emerging sea urchin industry.

Diving for sea urchins off the coast of Eden. Photo: Stefan Andrews, courtesy Great Southern Reef Foundation.

“They can’t give us any advice on the sea urchin,” he said. “I have done all that work and spent all that money. I had to tell my staff that probably they may not have work in three months.”

Walbunja man Wally Stewart is a traditional custodian, advocate for Aboriginal fishing rights, and a member of the applicant for the South Coast Native Title claim.

The claim covers land from Bundeena in southern Sydney to the Victorian border and extends three nautical miles offshore. It was lodged with the Federal Court of Australia in 2018.

“I am disappointed the commercial fishers got paid out for damaging our Sea Country, but I am glad they are out of it once and for all,” Mr Stewart said. “I am disappointed she isn’t talking about putting any money into the restoration which we urgently need.”

Mr Stewart said there were major problems with the ocean including the sea urchins and the growing population of seals eating tonnes of fish daily.

“It seems like native title holders are the only ones lobbying for restoration,” he said. “The others just want their golden handshake.”

The government is also beefing up resources to combat illegal, unreported or unregulated abalone fishing. It is recruiting eight senior officers and beginning a recruitment drive for up to 11 new fisheries officers across NSW.

This week it is introducing a bill to parliament calling for increasing the powers of fisheries officers around inspections and compliance checks, support for safer interactions in the field, improved evidence collection, more thorough investigations into illegal activity, and better support for environmental and habitat protection work.

Mr Morris said the $6355 share price offered was a “slap in the face when it has been created by mismanagement by DPIRD”.

Mr Stewart said he was “blaming the government for this”.

“They have been in bed with the industry and now they are in this predicament,” he said. “It has played Blackfella off against the abalone industry and we’ve been used as the scapegoat.”

Original Article published by Marion Williams on About Regional.

canberra.title: Controversial ‘widow tax’ dropped from Labor’s changes to negative gearing
canberra.snippet: Labor had dropped its so-called “widow tax” that was part of the May budget, following a public and political backlash over the planned m...
canberra.content:
Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson says Labor is doing a “patch-up job” on a bad budget. Photo: Tim Wilson.

Labor had dropped its so-called “widow tax” that was part of the May budget, following a public and political backlash over the planned measure.

But the Coalition says the government is simply trying to fix a mess it created for itself.

Tax reforms to negative gearing and the capital gains discount would have left a widow or divorcee without their tax concession if a property was transferred to just one partner’s name.

It appeared to be an unintended consequence of the tax changes, with the Federal Government promising to remedy it with new legislation.

That exposure draft legislation has now been released for consultation, and ensures those who gain sole ownership of an investment property through divorce or the death of a partner will keep the same negative gearing benefits.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said this new tranche of legislation implemented the reforms to negative gearing and capital gains tax announced in the budget, with some changes.

“These reforms will help level the playing field for first home buyers, preserve the gains investors have made, and support investment in new housing supply,” he said.

“The draft amendments build on the core legislation passed by the parliament in June, addressing a number of more complex issues and ensuring the changes appropriately apply to a range of specific taxpayer circumstances and structures.

Those changes include:

  • Preserving existing eligibility for negative gearing or treatment as a new build in certain circumstances, including for residential dwellings acquired from a spouse as a result of inheritance or relationship breakdown
  • Application of the CGT changes to attribution managed investment trusts, with further consultation to consider options to lessen compliance costs for fund managers
  • Exempting capital gains distributed to beneficiaries via genuine testamentary trusts, deceased estates and special disability trusts from the minimum tax on capital gains, consistent with exemptions from the minimum tax on discretionary trusts
  • Ensuring the CGT changes apply appropriately to taxpayers who are only Australian residents for part of the period they directly hold an asset
  • Ensuring the CGT changes do not inappropriately bring forward the taxing point for deferred gains as a result of certain CGT events.

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said the Coalition welcomed the measure, but described it as a “patch-up job” and added that Labor must ensure a thorough consultation process.

“We know already that there are widows who are being hit by Jim Chalmers’ higher taxes, but what he’s done is given an edict basically to the banks not to implement the law,” Mr Wilson said.

“So, of course, it should be done. It should have been done properly the first time; and the best way to do it is to make sure it goes through a process, make sure we get input from those who are impacted, and of course, legislate as quickly as possible.

“But this is the problem of what happens when you have a rushed budget. The government doesn’t understand what it’s doing.

“Now they’ve laid landmines all across the economy, and now they’re trying to diffuse them. Of course, we welcome the government trying to diffuse the landmines they’ve laid across the economy.

“We’d rather they not make the Australian economy full with landmines as a first position … so, I don’t really give huge points for a patch-up job for creating the problem and then trying to solve the problem they created.”

Senior Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie suggested the release of new draft legislation was embarrassing for the government.

“I think what we’re seeing with another backflip from Labor is confirmation of Labor’s economic incompetence,” Senator McKenzie said.

“The fact that nearly three months after the Federal Budget is handed down, we’re having to again have to fix up a mess of Labor’s making.”

Independent ACT senator David Pocock, who was a loud voice in drawing attention to the flaws in the original bill, welcomed the changes.

He said the exposure draft legislation appeared to tackle “many of the most urgent concerns” that had been raised about the initial bill.

“However, the timing for passage of this legislation is important,” Senator Pocock said.

“It is critical that lenders are able to consider preserved benefit in assessing loan serviceability in decisions they are making now and in coming months.”

canberra.title: Why the ACT Government wants to stop households from buying new gas appliances earlier
canberra.snippet: Parts of Canberra’s gas network might start being switched off from the mid-2030s as the ACT Government considers what additional l...
canberra.content:
Gas appliances hooked up to the network will no longer be an option in the Territory by 2045. Photo: Miguel_SR.

Parts of Canberra’s gas network might start being switched off from the mid-2030s as the ACT Government considers what additional laws are needed to phase out gas appliances.

A discussion paper’s been released outlining potential regulatory options to transition away from fossil-fuel gas by 2045, including improving consumer information, strengthening rental standards and limiting new gas appliance installations.

Already, new gas connections cannot be installed in residential, commercial or community facility land-use zones.

Gas users will need to be completely electric before the network is shut off.

“The ACT Government is now considering if gas appliance regulation is needed to support the most effective and least-cost pathways to support priority households [to] electrify and reduce fossil fuel gas use ahead of phase network decommissioning,” the paper stated.

“Some sections of the network may begin to be shut off from the mid-2030s onwards.”

According to the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO), Australian household and commercial gas use is expected to be basically non-existent by 2050.

The ACT Government is concerned that, without regulating gas appliances, Canberrans could buy gas appliances they’ll then need to replace with electric options before the gas appliance has reached its end of life (known as a stranded asset), or could be locked into increasing costs for running gas appliances as more people leave the network.

“With some sections of the network potentially being decommissioned from the mid-2030s onwards, new appliances may only be useable for 5-10 years,” the paper stated.

“An average expected lifetime for gas appliances [is] around 12 years.”

The paper stated regulation could reduce the time, resources and risks businesses faced in the gas transition by limiting their options.

Giving the example of banning the installation of new gas space heating within two years, it could mean installers would now know when a stream of work would end, give appliance retailers a timeframe to run down their stock levels, and give network operator Evoenergy greater certainty on when and where the electricity network will need to be built out.

As for rental properties, the paper noted that breakdowns of appliances for hot water, cooking, heating and cooling have to be repaired or replaced as soon as possible. However, gas appliances tend to be cheaper than electric options.

“This cost factor, combined with the short timeframe for replacement decisions, means it can be easier for landlords to do like-for-like replacement for gas appliances,” it stated.

“This could be a key decision point for government to intervene, requiring replacement with an electric appliance instead.”

Regulation could also restrict replacing centralised systems in apartments by owners’ corporations.

Network-connected gas appliances identified as potentially regulated include household and light commercial options (such as space heaters, water heaters, cooktops and gas pool heaters) and larger or custom-built appliances used in industrial and commercial settings (such as hot water, heating, automotive spray booths, coffee roasting and backup generators).

Options include providing information at the point of sale (such as when plastic shopping bags were phased out), mandating transition planning for gas appliance work, regulating what licensed gas fitters can install, regulating standards for rental properties, and prohibiting gas installation when a network section is identified for decommissioning.

Banning the sale of gas appliances – while possible – is not the government’s preferred pathway.

“It has significant barriers to successful implementation, including enforcement, compliance, and interstate trade,” the paper noted.

Climate Change, Environment, Energy and Water Minister Suzanne Orr said all feedback would help shape a draft regulatory framework and guide future community consultation.

“The ACT has already made strong progress in transitioning away from gas, but there is more to do to support households and businesses, particularly renters and low-income households, through this change,” she said.

“The government will work with the community to understand the challenges and opportunities for homes, businesses, industry, and community groups, ensuring everyone benefits from the energy transition.”

Stakeholder consultation is open from 5 August to 16 September. For more information, or to provide feedback on the discussion paper, visit Everyday Climate Choices.

australia.title: Nearly 1,500 properties bought using Australia’s first home buyers' 5% deposit scheme converted into investments
australia.snippet: New data shows the federal government scheme has been used by high-income borrowers, including one couple earning an annual $674,000 Get ...
australia.content:
The government’s 5% deposit scheme for first home buyers has enabled the purchase of nearly 1,500 properties that were turned into investments, new data shows.

The scheme is also helping hundreds of Australians earning more than $300,000 a year, after Labor stopped excluding high-income borrowers.

First-time buyers can borrow 95% of a property’s value and have the government guarantee the loan, waiving costly lenders’ mortgage insurance, under the scheme.

Housing Australia, which runs the program, provided the data in response to a Senate estimates question on notice in June.

From its launch in 2020 until May 2026, the scheme released 1,486 homes because they were converted into investment properties, the agency said.

The conversions were a small proportion of the 208,000 total guarantees issued over that time.

Barbara Pocock, the Greens’ housing spokesperson, said the scheme was supposed to help first home buyers on lower incomes to get a roof over their heads.

“It shouldn’t benefit the wealthy and property investors,” Pocock said.

Guardian Australia asked the housing minister, Clare O’Neil, whether investment purchases were undermining the scheme’s intention.

A spokesperson said: “When a participant transitions out of the scheme, and the government is no longer guaranteeing their mortgage, the owner is entitled to decide what they do with their home.”

If buyers stop living in the property, they are no longer covered by the guarantee and must negotiate with their bank but are not forced to sell or refinance.

Bob Tasevski, a Mortgage Choice broker, said buyers would typically try to avoid being forced off the guarantee as their bank would probably charge them the unpaid lender’s mortgage insurance.

“Banks generally wouldn’t waive that unless there’s a special reason for it,” Tasevksi said.

NAB’s executive for home ownership, Lin Lu, said the bank asked customers to advise if their circumstances changed.

“When this occurs, we’ll work with them to understand their individual situation and discuss the options available to them,” Lu said.

The government did not directly answer when asked if it could rule out the prospect of more 5% scheme buyers fraudulently renting out their purchases without notifying lenders or the government.

A spokesperson said Housing Australia monitored rental listings, property datasets, participants’ transaction activity and changes to addresses to ensure properties remained owner-occupied.

Booming popularity

The Albanese government amended the scheme so it no longer excluded high-income earners in October 2025. Since then, it had enabled more than 5,600 home purchases each month on average, compared with just over 3,400 the year before.

Prices of homes eligible for the scheme have since risen faster – and fallen more slowly – than the rest of the market.

Guardian Australia in July revealed one in three new participants was earning above the scheme’s previous annual income caps of $125,000 for singles and $200,000 for couples.

The new data shows the scheme had been used by 155 singles earning more than $300,000 and 92 couples earning over $400,000. The highest-earning recipient was a couple on more than $674,000.

The treasurer, Jim Chalmers, dismissed criticism of high-earners’ access on the ABC on Monday.

“There are some markets around the country, where people, even on relatively good incomes, have found it difficult to get a toehold in the market,” Chalmers said.

Participants in the scheme are in strong financial positions, with 89% ahead on their repayments, according to Housing Australia’s data. They were less likely to fall behind on loans than the average homebuyer.

Since the scheme began, 1,392 guarantees of the 207,000 had fallen more than 90 days behind on their loan and 436 of those were still in arrears by May.

Of the 45,300 homes bought under the scheme from its expansion up to May, just two households were in arrears, a separate answer revealed.

The government has only had to foot the bill on 13 defaults over the lifetime of the scheme, at a total cost of $604,537. Most of those claims emerged in the last 12 months.

While rising interest rates and falling house prices have added to the risk of defaults, fewer than 1% of all home borrowers across the country are in negative equity.

Do you know more? Email luca.ittimani@theguardian.com

australia.title: ‘Just an easy cash grab’: why Jetstar is charging customers for carry-on luggage
australia.snippet: Add-on fees such as the new overhead locker baggage charge can make it harder to compare air fares, experts say Get our breaking news ema...
australia.content:
Cut-price fares may now be merely a facade for seemingly endless add-on fees after Jetstar’s new carry-on luggage charge meant the airline joined a growing number monetising basic services in the sky.

The new structure, announced by Qantas’s low-cost carrier on Wednesday, will mean from next year tickets will only include one “under seat bag”, such as a backpack, handbag or laptop bag.

Customers with stowed carry-on luggage will face an additional layer of fees, building on costs for check-in baggage, preferred seats, cancellation rights and meals and snacks.

It is the latest pricing change in a sector where multiple airlines now even give passengers an option to pay to be next to a vacant seat, in a clever strategy that allows carriers to charge for tickets that do not otherwise sell.

In an extreme example of pricing changes, Canadian airline WestJet reconfigured its aircraft last year, requiring passengers to pay an extra fee if they wanted a seat that reclines.

Such changes are usually marketed by the airlines as a simplified, user-pay system that keeps entry level prices low for those looking for a cheap fare.

But Graeme Hughes, a consumer expert and adjunct associate professor at Griffith University, says it further obscures the checkout price.

“This allows Jetstar to broadcast the cheapest price, but of course those add-on costs are something which are going to hit you as you click through the booking process,” Hughes says.

“There will be frustration there for travellers because it means they can’t easily do an apple-for-apple comparison with other airfares.”

Andy Kelly, the campaigns director at the consumer advocacy group Choice, says Jetstar’s new policy is “just an easy cash grab, really”.

“Already, to choose seats could be over $20, around $50 if you want the ability to cancel your flight to get a credit, and then an additional $50 to join their loyalty program to get a discount,” he says.

“They just make it really hard for consumers to make an assessment of value and also to compare different products.”

European experience

The EU recently mandated that airlines – along with booking platforms and search engines – will have to display air fares that are inclusive of carry-on luggage at the outset of the booking process, to make it easier for consumers to compare prices.

The European Council introduced the mandate after fierce pushback from the airlines to an earlier proposal by the European parliament to give passengers the right to carry on a small case for free, as well as the free under seat bags currently permitted.

In its press release, Jetstar said its shift to a “size-based carry-on baggage model” was similar to other low-fare carriers around the world.

Jetstar also claimed the model helps keep fares low because “you only pay for what you need”.

Jetstar has tried to present the change as a positive development for travellers, but it is also following the lead of these overseas carriers in charging people to bring anything other than a small bag or item that can fit under the seat in front of them.

Dr Ian Douglas, an honorary senior lecturer at the University of New South Wales’ School of Aviation, says pretty much every low-cost carrier in Europe charges some sort of fee, including Ryanair and EasyJet.

“It’s a little sad we’ve gone straight to the Ryanair model because Jetstar is not Ryanair,” he says. “Jetstar is filling a gap in the Qantas network.

“If you want to go to the Sunshine Coast or Cairns [for example], it’s quite likely the offer will be Jetstar and not Qantas.”

Jetstar says the new fee will depend on the length of the flight and has acknowledged that fees may change. It can exceed $100 to carry an overhead bag on an overseas trip, according to Guardian Australia analysis of different Jetstar routes.

Ireland-headquartered Ryanair charges passengers €/£12-€/£36 if they pay when booking, or €/£20-€/£60 if they pay at the airport.

Britain’s EasyJet says its fees vary, including based on demand. Passengers who don’t pay in advance are charged £60 at the boarding gate.

The German low-cost carrier Eurowings charges basic-fare customers fees from €18 or £16 for “large” carry-on luggage.

In the US, leading low-cost carriers JetBlue and Southwest include a small personal item and a larger carry-on bag in their fares, while Frontier charges passengers based on their route.

australia.title: Virginia Bell rejects suggestion Palestinian group’s counsel ‘hijacked’ commission, inquiry hears
australia.snippet: Antisemitism royal commission also hears from former neo-Nazi who discovered ‘brotherhood’ was a ‘load of lies’ Get our breaking news ema...
australia.content:
Life in multi-ethnic Australia helped decouple a former skinhead from neo-Nazi groups as he discovered the brotherhood was “a load of lies”.

The unnamed witness offered his experience to the royal commission into antisemitism and social cohesion on Wednesday, on the same day the commissioner Virginia Bell rejected an assertion proceedings had been hijacked.

The witness said a somewhat isolated suburban upbringing as the child of British migrants pushed him toward right-leaning skinheads.

Those friendships, a period of “upheaval” in his life and conflict with a person from a minority background during his time in the defence force helped solidify a hardline supremacist stance.

But he said working in the wider community eventually helped him leave a neo-Nazi organisation, first for one year, and then in 2013 for good.

“I took a good hard look, and I’d also been doing some work in different places where I had been mixing with people of all different ethnicities,” he said.

“Some of these people of different ethnicities were the people that actually had my back and that showed some true brotherhood to me, and I decided that, yeah, [neo-Nazism] was all a load of lies.

“I love Great Britain as much as I love Australia. I still identify as very British, you know, but I also am very fervid in the belief that that’s got nothing to do with racist beliefs or anything like that.”

He suggested early intervention and openness to other cultures could have changed his course as a younger man.

Earlier on Wednesday, Bell reproached the authors of “truly abusive, Islamophobic emails” directed at a protest group’s counsel after Tuesday’s hearing.

Ragni Mathur SC, counsel for Australia Palestine Advocacy Network, asked a Jewish leader about the timeline of Israel’s response to Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack in the context of a protest held at the Sydney Opera House two days later.

Alex Ryvchin, the Executive Council of Australian Jewry’s co-chief executive, told the Australian newspaper it was “deeply concerning that these groups predictably used the opportunity to hijack an examination of lethal antisemitism for their clickbait theatrics and gratuitous slurs against Israel”.

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, later told News24 Mathur’s questioning was “disappointing”.

Bell, without naming Ryvchin, defended Mathur who “did not hijack this royal commission” and said counsel appearing should not become subject of attacks.

The hearing was also told the aesthetics, language and grievances of the radical right were capable of enticing youth without espousing a traditional political ideology

Modern neo-Nazism is more “perhaps narcissistic, more focused around their identity building” than before, the counter-terrorism expert Julian Droogan said.

Online content from groups such as involuntarily-celibates or manosphere creators was among the exploitative movements responsible, he said.

The political sociologist Joshua Roose said antisemitism and blaming Jews for grievances was alluring to the already disenfranchised.

Individual circumstances – financial, romantic and broader troubles – “pushed” many across the political spectrum towards antisemitic narratives, he said.

Hearings will continue on Thursday.

australia.title: Chris Bowen vows to override Queensland and NT to force renewables-powered AI datacentres
australia.snippet: Energy minister says Australian households and energy reliability will be protected by new federal legislation Get our breaking news emai...
australia.content:
The energy minister, Chris Bowen, says the federal government will override state governments that oppose new national rules on datacentres, with commonwealth legislation forcing new AI datacentres to be powered by renewable energy and banning those fuelled by gas.

Bowen said he expected his counterparts in Queensland and the Northern Territory – who had protested against the new federal rules at a meeting last week – to be unhappy with the move, but said the Albanese government was committed to powering the AI revolution with renewable energy.

“We will legislate as a commonwealth. The constitution is clear about the power of commonwealth legislation. I respectfully disagree with Queensland and the Northern Territory,” Bowen told the National Press Club on Wednesday.

The Australian Energy Market Commission warned that without rule changes such as those proposed by Bowen, the costs of bringing large datacentres online “will be paid for in part by customers” rather than big tech companies.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, last month pledged to legislate binding standards for AI datacentres, including on locations and energy use, with new national rules requiring them to rely on new renewable energy, minimise water use and maximise energy efficiency, pay for their grid connection costs and “put at least as much energy into our grid as they take out of it”.

Queensland and the NT last week opposed the changes in a meeting of state and federal energy ministers, despite all other states backing the plan. Queensland’s David Janetzki called the federal proposal “underdeveloped ideas that hand increased power to Canberra”.

The NT has proposed a major datacentre powered by gas from the controversial Beetaloo basin development.

But Bowen on Wednesday confirmed federal legislation would mandate the rules set out by Albanese. He said while gas had a “role to play” in firming up datacentre power use, “if a datacentre is proposed to only use gas, it will not meet the national minimum standards and it will not be allowed to register and will not be able to proceed”.

“While I always prefer to work with my state and territory colleagues, the commonwealth will not be standing by and letting a race to the bottom of states falling over themselves to attract datacentres, at the cost to household bills, reliability or emissions,” he said.

“We will use all the powers available to the commonwealth, including commonwealth legislation, to ensure that Australian households and Australian energy reliability is put first: even if some states have different ideas.”

The NT government was contacted for comment. Janetzki said his government “look forward to discussing” the issue at an upcoming national cabinet meeting on AI, but said his state “will not force uneconomic investment into the system”.

In a Q&A session after his speech, Bowen disputed the characterisation that Canberra would “force” states to comply, but stated that federal laws would override states.

“We’ll engage in our levers. The clearest one is obviously commonwealth legislation. We’re going down that road.”

Bowen said that while Albanese would soon confirm details of the federal legislation, new datacentres would have to prove the source of their renewables, how much power they were offsetting, that they would have backup power and that they would be “flexible” with use at peak times to stabilise the grid.

On Wednesday, the AEMC, the national body for the power grid, advised that datacentres should have to show renewables certificates. The AEMC said this was to ensure “their connection doesn’t tip the supply-demand balance and push up wholesale prices for everyone else”.

“Datacentre growth does not have to come at a cost to other consumers, but that depends on getting the settings right from the start,” the AEMC chair, Anna Collyer, said. “Our starting point is simple, this growth must not leave other consumers worse off.”

The AEMC said power operator Transgrid had seen “an unprecedented increase” in new connection requests in western Sydney, with about 8 gigawatts about to be connected to the grid – “on par with the entire average daily demand for NSW”.

The AEMC warned that, without changes to energy rules, grid connection costs for datacentres would be felt “across the consumer base at no clear consumer benefit”.

australia.title: Labor’s gambling reform friendless as Coalition withholds support amid drug and sex worker allegations
australia.snippet: Sarah Henderson says bill ignores gambling inducements, uniting parties and independents against controversial legislation Follow our Aus...
australia.content:
Labor will be forced to make major changes to its planned crackdown on online gambling advertising, as the Coalition, Greens and independents demand tougher rules to stop betting companies offering generous inducements as well as further limits on broadcast ads.

After a two-day inquiry including sensational evidence that gambling companies allegedly provided illegal drugs and access to sex workers to keep problem gamblers betting, the Coalition confirmed on Wednesday afternoon it would seek “crucial amendments” before agreeing to support the government’s legislation.

The Greens and key independents including David Pocock have all called for the bill to be significantly stronger, signalling a potential rerun of Labor’s Senate defeat on aged care reforms which was secured by the non-government parties teaming up.

“Labor’s gambling reform bill is riddled with deficiencies and must be significantly amended,” the shadow communications minister, Sarah Henderson, said, suggesting the opposition’s view the government was failing to take gambling harm seriously.

“The bill ignores gambling inducements which are causing immeasurable harm to some Australians. There is mounting evidence legislative action is required to combat predatory inducements which target high risk or vulnerable gamblers.”

Henderson also flagged changes to the limits and frequency of gambling ads, saying up to three per hour during children’s television programming was untenable and that she had serious concerns about opt-out rules for streaming platforms.

Guardian Australia has been told the communications minister, Anika Wells, met with Henderson on Wednesday to discuss the bill.

Liberal frontbencher Simon Kennedy is among Coalition MPs pushing for a stronger response, especially after evidence from former NRL player Luke Bateman and veteran anti-gambling campaigner Tim Costello this week.

They alleged problem gamblers had been supplied with cocaine, alcohol and sex workers, part of efforts from gambling company VIP managers to keep big spending punters betting as long as possible.

“Gambling addiction is taking an enormous toll on so many Australian families,” Henderson said.

“After three years of delay, deflection and deception over gambling reform, the Albanese government’s failings on this bill are inexcusable.”

The Greens communication spokeswoman, Sarah Hanson-Young, told Guardian Australia it was clear the bill would not pass parliament in its current form.

“This is a test for the prime minister,” she said.

“It is not party political or ideological at this point. It is a moral question.”

Opponents of Labor’s bill have pointed to a landmark inquiry report delivered by the late MP Peta Murphy in June 2023. Murphy’s committee recommended the government “prohibit all online gambling inducements and inducement advertising, and that it do so without delay”.

Labor has been already facing calls from within its own ranks for a tougher response. MPs Louise Miller-Frost and Alicia Payne told Guardian Australia on Wednesday the draft legislation should be significantly strengthened.

Non-Labor MPs could also vote to extend the inquiry, including to force big sporting codes including the AFL and NRL to attend hearings.

Pocock told Guardian Australia he welcomed the Coalition’s comments and would await details from Henderson.

“I hope Senate colleagues in the Coalition will also support my push for a national regulator, a full gambling advertising ban and an end to harmful inducements as recommended by the Murphy review,” he said.

”If the bill is amended to ban inducements and move to an opt-in arrangement for gambling advertising as the Coalition is proposing, it would be significantly strengthened and, based on what I’ve heard from Canberrans and experts, I would likely support.”

world.title: El Niño could push 50m people into acute hunger before end of next year
world.snippet: UN forecasters warn of worsening conditions in 45 countries currently experiencing severe food insecurity About 50 million people are lik...
world.content:
About 50 million people are likely to be pushed into acute hunger before the end of next year by the rapidly developing El Niño weather system, according to forecasting.

This is in addition to the hundreds of millions of people already facing dangerous levels of hunger, owing to years of drought in parts of Africa and pressure on food prices from the war in Iran.

Even if the forecast El Niño is less strong than some models predict, it will tip many countries over the edge, adding more than a fifth to the 225 million people in 45 countries currently in acute food insecurity, the UN’s World Food Programme (WFP) warned on Wednesday.

Central and South America, the Caribbean and southern Africa are likely to be worst affected, according to the analysis. In south and south-east Asia there is likely to be less rainfall than usual, which would cause serious problems for agriculture and farmers.

This year’s El Niño – a weather system that develops every few years in the Pacific Ocean and brings changes to rainfall patterns around the world – is shaping up to be the strongest in at least 70 years. Some are calling it a “super El Niño”, though this term is not officially recognised.

What is certain is that its impacts and strength are being strongly affected by the climate crisis. Earlier this year, experts said a strong El Niño could work in tandem with global heating to deliver the hottest year on record either this year or, more likely, in 2027.

Private sector forecasters have already warned of the impact of the gathering El Niño on global food prices, but the report published by the WFP is the first to look closely at global hunger. The WFP said it was hoping to reduce the effects of the extreme weather through early warning systems and “anticipatory” relief efforts, for which at least $80m (£60m) is budgeted.

The consequences will still be far-reaching, as farmers may take more than one season to exhaust their food supplies. In southern Africa, for instance, the main growing season stretches from October this year to March 2027, but it will be about nine months later, during the lean season following the harvest, that the worst impacts will bite.

“The biggest food security impact, in southern Africa, will be during the 2027 to 2028 lean season,” said Richard Choularton, the WFP’s director of the climate and resilience service.

Farmers should be somewhat cushioned by the lingering benefits of last year’s harvest, which was an unusually good one. “At the end of 2025, food prices were in favourable ranges, though there has been upward pressure from the war in the Middle East,” said Jean-Martin Bauer, the WFP’s director of food security.

During the 2015-16 El Niño, about 60 million to 100 million people were affected by acute food insecurity, the term WFP uses to denote hunger that falls below the level of famine. In those years, the WFP was not yet rolling out its updated anticipatory actions, so its experts hope this year’s extreme weather will have a lower impact even if the El Niño is more severe.

However, Choularton said efforts had been hampered by a lack of data, as some collection efforts had been cut for lack of funding.

The WFP’s data covers the 45 countries it works in where baseline estimates for food insecurity are available. There could be additional impacts outside these hard-hit areas.

Food prices could come under pressure across the world, as well as in the 45 countries examined, said Bauer. “This will also depend on the choices that exporting countries make. It’s very important to avoid a situation where large countries stop food exports,” he said. “At the regional level, there could certainly be high prices and [problems with] food access.”

In the UK and Europe, farmers have been warning of the impact of extreme heat and lack of rainfall on their harvests, with retailers braced for higher prices.

world.title: Wednesday briefing: ​How misinformation and ​a​ hardened immigration policy ​turned Ceuta ​into Europe’s ​latest ​flashpoint
world.snippet: In today’s newsletter: The past week shows how quickly images, rumours and ​right-wing political opportunism can eclipse the facts on the...
world.content:
Good morning. Last week, an estimated 72,000 migrants began crossing into a tiny Spanish enclave on the tip of Morocco. Within 24 hours, most of them had headed home. At least 88 people died after attempting the crossing, according to local officials. This isn’t the whole story of what happened over the last week, but the facts are worth remembering.

At an emergency meeting yesterday, EU interior ministers sought to draw a line under Ceuta, insisting that the passport-free Schengen area had never been at risk from the arrival of migrants at this scale. Despite this, much of the media coverage has suggested that events in Ceuta represent a territorial threat to Europe, sparking calls for greater security across the region’s borders.

It’s a pattern that has become familiar since the 2015 refugee crisis. As Europe has created fewer opportunities for migrants to legally cross its borders, people have tried to cross them illegally, resulting in dangerous bottlenecks, human tragedies, and a slew of spectacular images that the right has seized upon to justify draconian policies.

For this morning’s newsletter, I spoke to Daniel Trilling, a journalist who writes about refugees and migration, about the political actors trying to capitalise on Ceuta, and why tragedies like this are bound to keep happening. That’s after the headlines.

Five big stories

  1. Environment | Eight of the biggest oil companies amassed profits of more than $90bn (£67bn) in just three months as the Iran conflict sent energy prices soaring and the emissions-fuelled climate crisis caused deadly heatwaves.

  2. UK politics | Women should not feel pressurised into experiencing an “ideal birth”, the new health secretary, Yvette Cooper, has said, promising a root-and-branch reform of standards after several damning maternity scandals.

  3. Middle East | Jordan is convening an emergency meeting over an “imminent” threat of an Israeli takeover of the most important Muslim site in Jerusalem, with the potential to “trigger a religious conflict”.

  4. Ukraine | Russian strikes in and around Kyiv killed at least 14 people, ⁠injured 27 and ⁠damaged warehouses, ​emergency service officials said. Some reports put the death toll at 15.

  5. Ceuta | Hundreds of people have gathered in the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq, near the border with Spain’s Ceuta, flashing photos of their missing loved ones to passersby in the hope of tracking them down.

In depth: ‘The claim that this is some kind of invasion of Europe is entirely untrue’

On Thursday, a group of people roughly the size of Guildford’s population began crossing into Ceuta. Many of them swam around the border fence. Some drowned; others were crushed. Dozens died. “There were so many people in the sea. Everyone was trying to grab on to you to save themselves, and you were trying to escape and move forward so they wouldn’t drag you down or drown you,” one told the Guardian.

Most of these people were young men searching for work and hoping to build a better life for themselves. There are no reports suggesting any of them reached mainland Europe. “It’s very difficult for people without the right documents to travel from Ceuta to mainland Europe, and Spain has lots of experience returning people who cross without permission,” Trilling says. “So the claim that this is some kind of invasion of Europe is entirely untrue.”

Although Spain was reporting on Friday that most of these migrants had returned to Morocco, videos of men clambering on rocks and walking through Ceuta’s streets had already gone viral on social media, where they were amplified by right-wing voices. “Ceuta has been turned into a third world city in only 48 hours,” Tommy Robinson posted on X. Elon Musk, no stranger to sticking his oar into the politics of foreign nations, posted: “all military age males means it is an invasion”.

“By the time the images started circulating, the so-called crisis was over. But the political damage was already done,” Trilling says.

Why did so many people make the crossing?

A social media hoax, which hinged on a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported, seems to have played a pivotal role in encouraging the crossings. Instagram posts suggested Spain’s border with Morocco was opening up, TikTok videos showed people where to swim, and Facebook users began tracking coast guard patrols. It’s unclear who was behind these accounts, as several of them were deleted soon after the crossings. At a crisis meeting on Saturday, EU member states speculated that the events may have been coordinated.

As the hoax spread, Moroccan border surveillance dwindled to a minimum, allowing thousands of people to cross into Ceuta. Some analysts have suggested that Rabat, Morocco’s administrative capital, deliberately opened the border to protest Pedro Sánchez’s recent visit to Algeria (Morocco has a territorial dispute with the country). Others have pointed to Rabat’s increasingly toasty relationship with the Trump administration, which has clashed with Sánchez during the Iran war.

Hasn’t this happened before?

“The central problem is that European border policies have given countries like Morocco a means of exerting pressure on European states,” Trilling says. The EU has increasingly outsourced (“externalised,” in the policy lingo) border policing to non-EU countries, which have the power to loosen their borders whenever they choose. We’ve seen versions of Ceuta happen before: in 2021, Morocco allowed 10,000 people to cross into the territory during a diplomatic row with Spain. Turkey tried something similar on Greece in 2020, and Poland has long accused Belarus (a close ally of Russia) of encouraging migrants to cross into the Schengen area.

The EU has taken an increasingly hardline stance on migration since 2015. This has paradoxically helped to create some of the problems that politicians say they’re trying to solve. The fortification of security means that people are forced into taking illegal and unsafe routes where there might have been safe, legal routes previously. When border security is breached, it results in a sudden influx of people, and the kind of alarming images that we’ve seen this week, which are then used to justify even further restrictions. “The performance of control very often leads to precisely the sense in which things are out of control,” says Trilling.

How is the right capitalising on this?

Following the events in Ceuta, Nigel Farage wasted no time in resurrecting his pernicious “Breaking Point” poster from 2016, and he and Zia Yusuf, Reform’s spokesperson, have described those who made the crossing as “fighting-age males.” The term is one of the right’s favourite new ways to frame people crossing borders, depicting them as threats, while giving little thought to those who lose their lives or don’t fit the brief. By Monday afternoon, Farage had alighted on a new policy that would use the Royal Navy to “stop the boats once and for all”. We published a useful explainer on why this would probably violate international law.

It would be possible to dismiss this announcement as a last-ditch attempt to change the subject, considering the £5m gift that Farage currently seems to want to avert eyes from (and his impending byelection bin fight). But that would be missing the bigger picture. Ceuta has given the right a powerful new argument for why hardline immigration policies are common sense, and, by contrast, why a more pragmatic and humane approach to migration is foolish, harmful or, as one Spectator piece put it recently, the result of “luxury” beliefs.

This sort of language encourages centre-left parties to accept the right’s logic. Take, for example, Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, who was among 22 signatories to a letter on Saturday that suggested Spain’s liberal migration policies compromise Europe’s security. These policies have no application in Ceuta, but Merz will soon be trying to fight off the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) in state elections.

What happens next?

In a speech delivered from the White Cliffs of Dover on Monday, Andy Burnham pledged to be “relentless” in curbing small boats while building a system that offers “safe routes”. It marked a change from Starmer, whose attempts to appease would-be Reform voters culminated in his infamous “Island of strangers” speech. Still, it’s too early to say how Burnham will approach migration, and whether he will reopen routes that his predecessor closed.

“Time and again, the right has tried to claim that you can basically shut yourself off from the rest of the world and make these things go away,” Trilling says. “But they don’t go away. And Ceuta is a perfect example of that.”

What else we’ve been enjoying

  • I was really moved by these images from a summer camp for LGBTQ+ kids in Texas, a state where trans people have been regularly targeted and demonised. Michael

  • What do Feast, Viennetta, Magnum, Calippo, Twister and Cornetto have in common? They were all invented in the 15-year golden age of British ice-cream. Hettie

  • As a fair weather cyclist, I’ve had a smug summer, avoiding sardines-in-a-sauna style public transport on my bike. Reading about commuters on the heaving 17:46 from Euston has only confirmed this. Michael

  • “In our culture, we vilify vulnerability and valorise independence”, the author Emily Kenway writes in this thoughtful opinion piece about the family members who sustain our care system. Hettie

  • I for one have (obviously) always been a fan of the Turritopsis dohrnii, but at last the immortal jellyfish is getting proper recognition in this year’s Guardian invertebrate of the year competition. Michael

Sport

Cycling | The world time-trial champion, Marlen Reusser, took the overall lead in the Tour de France Femmes after winning the fourth stage from Gevrey-Chambertin to Dijon.

Football | Gianni Infantino’s authority was dealt a further blow after his No 2, the Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafström, called the failed World Cup private investment plan a “sad and reproachable series of events”.

Football | The Manchester United captain, Maya Le Tissier, said her team will “stick together” and be ready for the new Women’s Super League season, despite their head coach Marc Skinner departing.

The front pages

“Oil giants make $90bn from price surge as climate crisis engulfs Europe”, is the Guardian’s front page.

The Telegraph says “Setting free Pc Harper’s killers is ‘not justice’”, the Mail writes “9,300 domestic abusers set to be released”, Metro has “Jailed just last year … but my son’s killer already set freedom”, and the Sun’s take is “See you in court, PM”.

The FT splashes “Google assembles $200bn Wall Street machine to supply chips for Anthropic”, the i Paper has “Private firms may face ban on profiteering to make care homes cheaper” and the Express writes “How many more lives will you risk by doing nothing?” The Times, on fiscal rules, says “Borrowing splurge in bid to boost economy”.

The Latest

Is Gianni Infantino’s time up as Fifa president?

Gianni Infantino’s reign as Fifa president is in severe peril after the collapse of his plans to sell off parts of the World Cup to private investment. Many Concacaf countries are considering following Europe’s lead by formally removing their support for Infantino, and there are widespread calls to remove him from his post. Lucy Hough speaks to columnist Jonathan Liew. Watch it on YouTube.

Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron

The Upside

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Once the soundtrack to postwar optimism and excess, Côte d’Ivoire’s dance music scene is evolving, thanks to TikTok and street dance battles.

Seven years after the death of its biggest star, DJ Arafat, a new generation of artists and dancers are reinventing the coupé-décalé genre, with the new high-energy biama movement winning over young fans and social media users alike. Eromo Egbejule visits a 400-strong neighbourhood dance arena in Abidjan, where a local rapper calls the craze “a dance for the immature”.

Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday

Bored at work?

And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

  • Quick crossword

  • Cryptic crossword

  • Wordiply

world.title: Hundreds in Morocco gather near Ceuta border in anxious wait for missing loved ones
world.snippet: People hope to see friends or relatives among those still returning as death toll from mass crossing nears 100 Hundreds of people have ga...
world.content:
Hundreds of people have gathered in the northern Moroccan town of Fnideq, near the border with Spain’s Ceuta, flashing photos of their missing loved ones to passersby in the hope of tracking them down.

Their perch was the same small tranche of land that made headlines around the world last week as extraordinary scenes emerged of about 72,000 people making their way into Ceuta, a tiny Spanish territory in north Africa.

On Tuesday, as interior ministers from across the EU joined an emergency videoconference to grapple with the lingering tensions, the focus on the Moroccan side of the border with Ceuta was on the harrowing death toll.

At least 88 people have died in Ceuta, according to local officials, and another 11 in Morocco, while dozens of others remain missing.

“I have just one son,” said Hadijja, who had been waiting at the border since Saturday, scanning the steady stream of returnees for any sign of her 23-year-old son. “I haven’t had any news of him; he’s not answering his mobile phone.”

She had travelled to the border from her home in Tangier, surmising that her unemployed son was among those who had made the crossing. “He didn’t tell me he was going to cross,” she said. “This is a tragedy.”

An estimated 70,000 people who arrived late last week in Ceuta had been returned to Morocco in recent days, Spain’s interior minister said Tuesday.

Referencing posts on TikTok, Facebook and WhatsApp that had claimed Morocco was letting people cross the border, people arrived at Fnideq by foot or packed into buses and cars as they joined the surge of people crossing into Spain.

Madrid sprang into action, working with Rabat to return the vast majority of those who crossed within 48 hours, even as it fended off a political crisis sparked by calls for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen free-movement zone.

As they returned to Moroccan soil, some said they had come home voluntarily. “I was hungry for days and filled with fear,” said Abselam, 19, from Kenitra in north-western Morocco.

A Ceuta resident had eventually taken him in, giving him food and a place to sleep, before he decided to return home. “It’s not worth it, there aren’t jobs for everyone.”

Others said they had been forced out of the Spanish territory. “The police surrounded a group of us and escorted us all the way towards the border,” said Simo, 21, from Tetuan. “We didn’t really have a choice.”

In recent days, NGOs across Spain have voiced concerns that some of those who crossed into Ceuta and who were eligible for international protection were being returned before being allowed to exercise their right to request asylum.

On Tuesday the Spanish government estimated that 2,000 people who had made the crossing were still in Ceuta. The tally includes at least 862 children who have been registered as unaccompanied minors, as Unicef Spain warned that dozens more could still be wandering the city’s streets unprotected.

“Many small children crossed over; we don’t know how many have disappeared,” Susana Hidalgo, a migration expert for the organisation, told the broadcaster TVE. The result was a “tremendously difficult” situation in Ceuta.

“There are many families on the other side of the border looking for their sons and daughters,” she said, while in Ceuta “there are 10- and 12-year-old children asking for phones so they can call their mothers and tell them they’re OK.”

Spanish police said on Tuesday they had set up an office in Ceuta to gather reports of missing people.

The concerns over the fate of unaccompanied children in Ceuta were heightened on Tuesday after Spanish media published a video that appeared to show a boy age 12 crying as he begged a soldier not to send him back to Morocco. After several bystanders intervened, pointing out that Spanish law impeded children from being deported alone, the operation – which played out just metres from the border – was halted.

Days after the sudden influx, questions continue to linger as to what led to the mass crossing. Morocco has faced mounting accusations over the role it may have played. “People felt that this, if not orchestrated, was at least encouraged or permitted by Morocco,” Juan Jesús Vivas, the long-serving conservative leader of Ceuta, said earlier this week.

The insinuation was rejected by a senior Moroccan official. “It’s simplistic to say that Morocco should just have used force to stop them. That is to completely misunderstand this phenomenon,” the official told AFP.

“At a certain point, the Moroccan law enforcement forces could no longer confront the migrants because the numbers were very large” and because “the pull effect was very strong,” he added. “Could Spain, seeing them coming, have done something to stop them simply using weapons and security forces? That’s not possible.”

In a statement published on Sunday, Morocco’s interior ministry laid blame with the “exploitation of the digital sphere” and “the spread of misinformation” to explain the mass crossing.

Spanish intelligence sources have suggested the influx could be traced to a hoax that had swiftly spread across social media after a Spanish supreme court ruling that migrants arriving by sea could not be summarily deported.

The Moroccan official said Rabat had sought to warn Madrid about the repercussions of the ruling. “We started engaging with the Spanish side around 22-23 July, when the networks began talking about this,” the official told AFP. “We explained that this ruling was going to create a problem. And it did create a problem.”

The claim was rejected by Spain’s migration minister, Elma Saiz. “At no point was there any evidence, any report that alerted us to the magnitude of this unprecedented event,” she told reporters in Madrid.

The uncertainty hovering over what exactly transpired extended to Fnideq, where the relatives gathered at the border spoke in hushed tones of what could have happened to their loved ones.

Many held on to hope, citing the trickle of good-news stories that had emerged in recent days, such as that of Fatima, who had spent the day waiting at the border with her family for a glimpse of her brother, who had crossed into Ceuta days earlier.

“My brother’s phone had run out of battery, but yesterday he borrowed the phone of a Spaniard to call me,” she said. “He told me he would come back this morning, so here we are waiting. I’m sure he’ll arrive soon.”

world.title: Stronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen says
world.snippet: European Commission president says work needed in five areas of migration control including returning more people The president of the Eu...
world.content:
The president of the European Commission has called for action to strengthen Europe’s borders after tens of thousands of people arrived and quickly left the Spanish territory of Ceuta, triggering a furious row between Madrid and other European countries.

In a letter to Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, on Monday, Ursula von der Leyen said: “From this incident, it is clear that we must do more to further strengthen our borders at critical points, including vigilant monitoring and the use of physical barriers where needed.”

She praised the Spanish socialist leader’s swift handling of the crisis, after the vast majority of migrants left Ceuta and Spanish officials began installing a 500-metre (1,640ft) floating barrier at the border ‌with Morocco. “Order has been restored and the returns system in place worked,” she wrote in the letter.

Spain ⁠estimates that about 69,500 migrants ​have returned to Morocco over the past four days, exceeding initial estimates of 50,000 having arrived in the enclave in north Africa on Thursday. Authorities in Ceuta reported that 88 people died trying to reach the territory, while at least 11 deaths have been recorded in Morocco.

Ceuta and Melilla, another Spanish enclave, have the EU’s only land borders with Africa. There are periodic surges in attempted crossings to both cities, although neither permits onward free movement to the EU as they are outside the border-free Schengen zone.

EU interior ministers will hold emergency talks on Tuesday, which von der Leyen said would be a chance to draw lessons from the crossings.

She said the EU should double down on five areas: strengthening cooperation with non-EU countries to prevent migration; stronger external borders; implementing early warning systems; dismantling smuggling networks; and boosting returns of people with no right to stay.

Italian media reported that Giorgia Meloni’s government wanted to accelerate the opening of offshore migration centres, which Europe’s top human rights expert recently said risked becoming “human rights black holes”.

The EU opened the door to offshore detention centres in June in an unprecedented departure from legal norms as part of a law aiming to increase the deportations of people with no legal right to stay.

Amid heavy criticism of the EU’s divided response to the Ceuta border crossings, von der Leyen stressed that Spain could access EU funds as well as support from the Frontex border agency. So far Madrid has not requested the assistance of Frontex.

The crossings – seized on by far-right politicians across Europe – have exposed deep divisions over migration that have left Spain’s leader isolated.

Over the weekend, Sánchez criticised other governments for failing to support Spain, after Italy and Denmark led calls for its temporary exclusion from the Schengen zone. Sánchez said such an attitude was “driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance or political interest” and contrary to European and humanitarian law “and the principles of solidarity that bind us together”.

Italy and Denmark organised a letter signed by 20 other EU member states that appeared to blame the crisis on Sánchez’s decision to regularise the status of 500,000 migrants without documents. “We have a duty to effectively deter and relentlessly combat illegal migration,” the 22 leaders wrote, arguing for the need to address “all policies that can serve as pull factors, such as the regularisation of [a] very large number of irregular migrants”.

EU member states favouring a tough approach to migration are expected to raise the issue of “pull factors” on Tuesday. “There is some concern that the regularisation of 1.2 million people can be used to paint a picture that the door is open,” an EU diplomat said, referring to the approximate number of people who applied for regularisation under the 2026 Spanish government programme.

Academic research has found no evidence of a pull effect from regularisation programmes on arrivals of irregular migrants.

Michele LeVoy, the director of Picum, an umbrella group that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants, said regularisation programmes had been criticised by EU governments for the last two decades. “If an EU country offers regularisation possibilities, other member states believe that it may invite secondary movement [onward movement to other EU member states] – that is what EU member states don’t want and that explains most likely the harsh response.”

Amid widespread suspicion that Morocco helped fuel the crisis, von der Leyen described the country as “an important strategic partner”, especially in combating “illegal migration”.

Officials said that before the Ceuta crossings, the European Commission was looking to upgrade the EU’s diplomatic relationship with Morocco to a “strategic and comprehensive partnership”. The EU already has similar wide-ranging agreements with Egypt and Tunisia, which include pledges to stem migration, but which have been heavily criticised by rights groups.

Von der Leyen wrote: “On anything related to Ceuta and Melilla, we could enhance border management early-warning systems and improve our technical and financial support to Morocco.”

Rights groups said people seeking work or fleeing persecution needed routes to move safely. LeVoy said: “On Ceuta, political games are being played over the lives of people on both sides of the border – those who hope for a better life, and those who are made to fear a so-called ‘invasion’. But what happened in and around Ceuta is fundamentally the result of Europe’s inaction on decent work permits and other regular pathways and the dismantling of its asylum systems.”

world.content:
Dozens of people died attempting to reach the Spanish enclave of Ceuta after an estimated 50,000 crossed from Morocco last week. The incident has led to a political crisis in Spain and criticism from EU countries.

Lucy Hough speaks to the Guardian’s European community affairs correspondent, Ashifa Kassam – watch on YouTube
